doc.title: Sheryl Bailey interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 24, 2023

title: Arts education for everyone, even those who do not go professional
summary: Bailey says first-year college is exploration and that music skills like problem solving transfer to any life; no one is too old to learn.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Have you ever had students that were, you know, they were pretty good but they didn’t seem — as you describe — to really love it? And have you felt like you need to tell them either you have to love this so much that you can’t do anything else, or maybe you should go and do an other kind of — pursue something else? I mean you can’t make people love something.

No you can’t. I think that is part of the journey. And in terms of even thinking about on a collegiate level just across the board, that first year of college for almost everybody is exploring and finding yourself. And maybe you’re going to go through that and you’re going to realize, maybe this isn’t for me, this isn’t what I thought. I think that’s going to be true for — really that first year is the first time you’ve been away, first time you’ve been alone, trying to find your identity and maybe you find it. But at the same time the — what we learn, so beyond being on the collegiate level for a profession, a big thing that was important that my mother also taught me is we can put it say music is for everybody but education is for everybody for the longevity of your life. Developing your intelligence and developing your skills is something you use all your life. So even if you come to this — you go through this process and you go hey I’m not going to be a professional musician, the skills that you learn, problem solving, time management, all of this is translatable. And that’s why arts education is so important on all levels. Not to make the next, you know, Chick Corea or Keith Jarrett. Do we all have to be thinking about creating virtuosos? We need to be sharing what the discipline and the art form is, and that’s for everybody, wherever they want to come into it. And I think that’s the thing. Some people will go, “I’m too old to learn an instrument.” I’m like, “Somebody told you that. That’s not true. Quit telling yourself that. It’s for everyone.” So —
